articles.title: Recorde da Anthropic em estreia na bolsa de valores conseguirá impedir o estouro da bolha da IA? | G1
articles.standfirst: O preço inicial da ação será de US$ 83 quando começar a ser negociada nesta quinta-feira. Com esse preço, o valor de mercado da Anthropic é estimado em US$ 1,5 trilhão.
articles.summary: O preço inicial da ação será de US$ 83 quando começar a ser negociada nesta quinta-feira. Com esse preço, o valor de mercado da Anthropic é estimado em US$ 1,5 trilhão.
articles.body:
Foi em novembro de 2020 que, em algum lugar de São Francisco, nos Estados Unidos, uma mulher chamada Daniela Amodei telefonou para uma amiga, pedindo conselhos.

Daniela supervisionava a segurança e as políticas da OpenAI , uma das empresas de inteligência artificial (IA) mais conhecidas do mundo.

Mas Daniela e seu irmão Dario, que também trabalhava lá, tinham dúvidas sobre os níveis de segurança na OpenAI . Eles pensavam que talvez fosse hora de sair.

Então, ela fez o que muitos fazem quando não conseguem tomar uma decisão: ligou para uma amiga. A resposta desta foi direta e objetiva: "Você não precisa falar comigo ao telefone. Você já sabe a resposta."

Os irmãos Amodei e alguns outros colegas se demitiram. Juntos, eles criaram uma empresa concorrente, a Anthropic.

Seis anos depois, a Anthropic, criadora do modelo de IA Claude, prevê receitas de US$ 52 bilhões em 2026 e US$ 135 bilhões em 2027, de acordo com estimativas de analistas.

Nesta quarta-feira (18/11), a empresa conseguiu a maior oferta pública inicial (IPO, na sigla em inglês) da história em sua estreia na Nasdaq , bolsa de valores em Nova York, superando o recorde anterior, da SpaceX de Elon Musk.

O preço inicial da ação será de US$ 83 quando começar a ser negociada nesta quinta-feira na Nasdaq. Com esse preço, o valor de mercado da Anthropic está avaliado em US$ 1,5 trilhão .

Esses valores são superiores aos informados pela empresa no início deste mês. A estimativa inicial era de que suas ações seriam vendidas por um valor entre US$ 70 e US$ 78, o que colocava a avaliação da companhia em até US$ 1,3 trilhão. Mas a demanda por ações da Anthropic foi grande no IPO de quarta-feira.

A oferta pública inicial ocorreu em um momento crucial, quando muitos se perguntam se, em meio à crescente preocupação com o potencial da IA, a bolha do setor está dando sinais de estouro.

Se antes os investidores apostavam tudo em uma revolução tecnológica que rivalizaria com as ferrovias, o automóvel, a eletricidade e a internet no impacto da inovação, alguns agora estão cautelosos, em meio a argumentos de que os preços da IA cairão à medida que a tecnologia se tornar mais comum.

Também há preocupações de que uma parcela considerável do investimento em IA seja composta por gigantes da tecnologia investindo umas nas outras.

As ações de empresas que fornecem a capacidade computacional bruta por trás da IA, como Coreweave e Nebius, viram seu valor cair pela metade, enquanto até mesmo a poderosa Nvidia perdeu sua coroa de empresa mais valiosa do mundo, com suas ações caindo 30% — uma queda impressionante de US$ 2 trilhões em valor.

Será que o IPO da Anthropic conseguirá reinflar a bolha? Ou será lembrado como o último suspiro de uma explosão que caminha para o colapso?

Painel na Bolsa de Valores de Nova York anuncia que Anthropic estava preparando IPO — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Em um evento na semana passada, o CEO (diretor executivo) da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, disse ao CEO do JPMorgan Chase, Jamie Dimon, que seu princípio orientador é: "Nunca deixar sua empresa valer um único dólar a mais do que realmente vale".

Há um ditado antigo que diz que, em uma corrida pelo ouro, você deve comprar empresas que vendem as ferramentas, em vez daquelas que apostam tudo na descoberta do metal.

No caso da Anthropic, as empresas de ferramentas são as fabricantes de chips, as construtoras de centros de dados e as fornecedoras de energia. Mas a Anthropic é, sem dúvida, o próprio ouro, segundo Fiona Cincotta, analista do mercado financeiro.

"Acho que a razão pela qual este IPO é tão importante é basicamente porque representa a primeira oportunidade para investidores públicos acessarem uma empresa focada exclusivamente em IA", afirmou à BBC, acrescentando que ofertas anteriores se concentraram em componentes e estruturas como semicondutores, chips e centros de dados.

"Esta é a primeira vez que conseguimos, de fato, acessar o provedor de IA."

O valor de uma empresa depende quase inteiramente da previsão de lucros futuros.

Estarão os usuários atuais e futuros da IA dispostos a pagar o suficiente para justificar os trilhões gastos em chips, centros de dados, energia e funcionários — alguns dos quais podem receber salários anuais superiores a US$ 100 milhões?

"A inteligência artificial certamente está em uma bolha financeira. Embora os LLMs [grandes modelos de linguagem] ofereçam utilidade genuína e, sem dúvida, vieram para ficar, a lógica econômica não fecha", afirmou Gary Marcus, professor emérito da Universidade de Nova York, em uma palestra no início deste ano.

"Quanto mais empresas criam modelos de IA, mais a tecnologia se torna uma commodity, eliminando vantagens competitivas significativas e reduzindo os preços."

Até o momento, as taxas de crescimento da receita da Anthropic são extraordinárias. Mas elas escondem um problema em potencial: cerca de um quarto dessa receita veio de apenas algumas empresas, entre elas o Google e a Amazon.

A empresa também está concentrada nos EUA, que representam dois terços de sua receita.

Existe também um impressionante ciclo de financiamento dentro do mundo da IA. Por exemplo, a Anthropic tem acordos para comprar ou arrendar centenas de bilhões de dólares em chips e poder computacional de um grupo seleto de empresas, incluindo Broadcom, Google e Amazon.

Muitas dessas empresas também são investidoras da Anthropic e grandes clientes de seus produtos.

Os irmãos Dario e Daniela Amodei fundaram juntos a empresa. — Foto: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images via BBC

Não são apenas alguns investidores de Wall Street que questionam se a IA é tudo aquilo que se diz. Nas ruas, as pessoas também têm suas preocupações.

Com os EUA impulsionando boa parte do crescimento global da IA, a reação à tecnologia — que ameaça substituir milhões de empregos e consumir vastas quantidades de energia e água — esteve presente nas recentes eleições de meio de mandato ( midterms ).

Muitas regiões dos EUA aprovaram moratórias para o desenvolvimento de centros de dados, e muitos candidatos considerados próximos das grandes empresas de tecnologia viram essa associação como um obstáculo político em vez de uma vantagem.

Alguns democratas se opuseram publicamente ao desenvolvimento de centros de dados e venceram.

Além disso, o até então CEO da fabricante de chips Nvidia Jensen Huang renunciou na semana passada após admitir ter sido "infiel" à sua esposa, na sequência de relatos de que teria tido um caso com uma suposta espiã chinesa, Alice Huang.

A queda dramática de Huang e a desvalorização de 30% das ações da Nvidia em relação ao seu pico deixaram os investidores em IA em busca de um novo queridinho para o sucesso da IA que sustentou o mercado de ações dos EUA e, possivelmente, grande parte de sua economia nos últimos dois anos.

Se a Anthropic e seu CEO forem mesmo os novos queridinhos da IA, eles representarão uma imagem diferente da do otimista e incansável Huang, com sua jaqueta de couro.

Enquanto Huang desejava que o desenvolvimento da IA continuasse a todo vapor, a Anthropic foi construída com base em receios sobre os níveis de segurança e responsabilidade que os ex-funcionários da OpenAI observaram no desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia capaz de mudar a sociedade.

Amodei alertou que as capacidades da IA podem viabilizar o desenvolvimento de armas biológicas, a vigilância em massa, o autoritarismo e a substituição de milhões de trabalhadores de escritório que pagam impostos.

Ele pediu uma desaceleração em seu desenvolvimento, pois seus poderes estão crescendo a uma taxa tão exponencial que muito em breve poderão escapar de qualquer supervisão humana.

Dito isso, suas declarações tidas como paternalistas foram recebidas com ceticismo por aqueles que apontam que o desenvolvimento de novos modelos mais poderosos pela Anthropic não demonstra nenhum sinal da desaceleração como a que ele defende para o restante da indústria.

Apesar de todas as preocupações, assim como aconteceu com a SpaceX , a expectativa e o "FOMO" (sigla que representa em inglês o medo de ficar de fora de algo relevante, ou "fear of missing out") em relação a um momento inegavelmente importante no desenvolvimento tecnológico e talvez humano fizeram com que o interesse de compra na estreia da Anthropic na bolsa fosse tão alto.

A demanda por ações da empresa excedeu em mais de seis vezes o número de ações oferecidas. Mas tamanha procura inicial não diz muito sobre o retorno a longo prazo.

Usando a SpaceX como exemplo novamente, as ações subiram quase 70% a partir de seu IPO, de US$ 135 para US$ 225. Atualmente, as ações da SpaceX estão cotadas a US$ 145.

O IPO da Anthropic pode injetar um pouco de ar fresco no que alguns ainda consideram uma bolha.

Eileen Burbidge, fundadora da Passion Capital, empresa de investimentos em tecnologia, é uma das pessoas que rejeitam a ideia de que a IA seja uma bolha prestes a estourar.

"Talvez o crescimento da bolha tenha diminuído um pouco, mas, na verdade, eu não diria que ela está prestes a estourar", afirma Burbidge. "Acho que esse IPO pode significar que todos podem voltar a acelerar."

Duas coisas podem ser verdadeiras ao mesmo tempo. O IPO da Anthropic pode ser um sucesso estrondoso — o FOMO é uma emoção poderosa nos mercados financeiros. Mas seu sucesso não apagará a constatação de que nem todas as empresas, investidores e cidadãos enxergam na IA uma resposta infalível para os problemas da humanidade.

articles.title: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
articles.summary: Canva is adding a new toggle that turns off its AI-powered features, including Magic Expand and its prompt-based editing tools.
articles.body: Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot. This toggle doesn’t turn off every AI-powered feature on Canva, however. That includes Canva’s background remover and its Magic Grab tool, which lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else. Canva says these tools will stay on because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.” [Image: The toggle still turns off many of Canva’s other AI features, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes, and more. Since Canva’s big push into AI in 2023, some users have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and asked for ways to turn them off. Canva has only continued to expand on its AI-powered image-editing suite since then, by rolling out a prompt-powered editing update in April and launching its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month. You can also now switch a toggle to see less AI content in Canva’s content library. Switching this option on means you’ll see human-created content first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements. Canva says a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content, and that any design that uses one of these elements will have an AI label in its metadata. To turn off Canva’s AI features, head to Profile > Settings > Permission, and then toggle off Enable generative AI features. You can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and then turning on the option to show less AI content. These switches are available to both free and paid users.

articles.title: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
articles.summary: For Anthropic, today is a years-in-the-making IPO that’s set to beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised more than $81 billion.
articles.body: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone. Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power. One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight. Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure. Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.” The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi. Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog. Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.” Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?” Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement. But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority. Instead, Anthropic’s structure looks more like the kind of founder-centric setup that Silicon Valley favors — like Mark Zuckerberg with Meta, and Elon Musk with SpaceX. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. “Neither the Trust or the trustees have any decisionmaking authority … over day to day decisions,” said Hamza Chaudhry, who leads AI and national security at the Future of Life Institute. “So I do not have strong hopes for the LTBT being a key mechanism for governance after they go public.” The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat. Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.” Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.” Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September. This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.” --- Are you a current or former Anthropic employee? Contact me via Signal at haydenfield.11 on a non-work device with tips. --- On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.” The former Anthropic employee said he felt he had initially “drunk the Kool-Aid” about Anthropic needing to come in first place in the AI race for a safe outcome but then grew disillusioned, realizing that the race to the top did not “warrant the cost imposed” — namely, that one company should not be able to “unilaterally” decide to pursue RSI. (Amodei has stated publicly that “left unchecked, [RSI] could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”) “It’s pretty ridiculous that private companies are building a new form of intelligence on track to be more powerful and influential on the planet than humans and are doing that with less oversight, in many ways, than taco trucks currently have,” the former employee said. Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.

articles.title: Sam Altman on whether Jensen Huang should come back to Nvidia: I wish Jensen the best, but I don’t think the world needs...
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has once again stayed out of the debate over whether Jensen Huang should return as Nvidia CEO.
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has once again stayed out of the debate over whether Jensen Huang should return as Nvidia CEO. Speaking at the NYT DealBook Summit, Altman praised the Nvidia co-founder but made it clear he did not want to add to the noise around his exit. "I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don't think the world needs another set of random opinions on what's going to happen here," Altman said.The comments come a week after Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, and after the company's board said it has no plans to bring him back.Altman did, however, make a case for what Huang means to the chipmaker. "Jensen is the guy who built this company from scratch," he said. "He deeply understands it. His personal relationships are the reasons that everyone is willing to do business."His view carries weight. OpenAI is one of the biggest buyers of Nvidia's AI chips, and the two companies are tied together through a major investment deal.Sam Altman's own 2023 ouster shapes his view of Jensen Huang's exitFor Altman, this is personal. OpenAI's board fired him as CEO in November 2023, only to reinstate him within days after employees and investors pushed back. He said that experience gave him more empathy for Huang."One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory here or there," he said.This is the second time this week Altman has sidestepped the question. At the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday, he was asked directly whether Huang should be reinstated. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," he said, adding that Huang has "long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws."At the same event, Altman said he has "personal strong empathy" for Huang and described Nvidia as "a behemoth of a company" that people still trust.When Huang later posted a statement on X offering to come back, Altman's only public response was a green heart emoji in the replies.Jensen Huang has offered to return as Nvidia CEOHuang stepped down after reports that he had affairs with an Nvidia employee and with a businesswoman who US intelligence has determined is linked to Chinese intelligence. In his X post on November 17, his first public statement since resigning, Huang said he had made "serious mistakes" in his personal life and would cooperate with the board's independent investigation.He also left the door open. "Nvidia is a once-in-a-generation company," Huang wrote, adding that he would be "honored" to return as CEO if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America.His allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street have been campaigning for his return. US President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" Huang coming back. Not everyone agrees. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Huang should not return, pointing to concerns over Nvidia's advanced chips reaching China.Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen HuangNvidia's board has shut that door for now. Opening the company's quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, board chair Harvey Jones said the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."Chief financial officer Colette Kress is running the company as interim CEO while a search firm looks for a permanent replacement. At an all-hands meeting on Wednesday, she told employees the company's ambition would not change. "Just remember, we've got this," she said.The numbers back her up, at least on paper. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion for the quarter ending October, ahead of Wall Street estimates. Its market value, though, has slid from close to $6 trillion a month ago to around $3.66 trillion.Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress on December 1, while an outside law firm continues its investigation into his conduct.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
articles.summary: Anthropic has started trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, and began trading at $111.50 per share.
articles.body: Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” at $111.50 per share, up from its initial $83 per share price that put company’s value at around $1.5 trillion. The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public. In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders. While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters. “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.” Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic. Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

articles.title: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, representing more than $80 billion in new capital raised.
articles.body:
Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.

Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.

The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch , “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”

The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.

In a speech before the opening bell , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

articles.title: Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%
articles.summary: Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero em...
articles.body:
Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030.

Why it matters : Other tech giants have reported rising emissions as they race to build data centers, but Meta is going a step further by explicitly reconsidering its climate deadline.

Driving the news : The just-released sustainability report of the tech giant, one of North America's largest data centers operators , shows just how much growth in the AI industry is outpacing any efficiency gains.

Meta executives said they were "re-evaluating" the 2030 goal, first announced in 2020 when the company was still known as Facebook and before the generative AI boom.

They didn't specify what changes they're considering or when they'll make a decision.

By the numbers : Meta's electricity use jumped 35%, comparable to other tech giants. But Meta's emissions increase of 45% is far higher than its peers, Google (18%), Amazon (16%) and Microsoft (25%).

What they're saying: "When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned," wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability.

"The reality has been far more complex."

Zoom out : The race among tech giants to dominate AI is pushing their climate goals into the backseat, even as they continue investing heavily in clean energy.

State of play : Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal, though less than half that capacity is generating electricity so far.

The intrigue : Meta's report says it may turn to natural gas plants to power data centers when utilities can't deliver electricity fast enough — even though such projects are already underway.

It's also seeking to offset some of the methane emissions associated with its natural gas use by paying for cleaner gas production elsewhere.

Reality check : Meta's 45% emissions increase doesn't yet reflect the full impact of some of its biggest planned natural gas projects, suggesting its footprint could grow considerably more.

In Louisiana, utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas-fired generating units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts to serve Meta's data centers.

Separately, Ohio regulators approved a 200-megawatt gas plant built specifically to power Meta's data centers, while research firm Cleanview identifies a 521-megawatt gas project under construction for Meta in Utah.

articles.title: Brighton Anthropic founder to become billionaire
articles.summary: Jack Clark is one of seven founders of Anthropic - the only one not from North America.
articles.body:
A man from Brighton who helped to set up the AI company Anthropic, which made its stock market debut on Thursday, is set to become a billionaire.

Jack Clark was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he initially worked in communications, later becoming its policy director.

The company behind Anthropic, Claude, was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Clark is the only one of the founder not from North America and is the head of public benefit at Anthropic, also leading the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

He studied English literature and creative writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

Nigel Marshall, who taught Clark philosophy at Varndean College, said he was a "very bright person".

He said: "I do remember him. He was incredibly articulate, interested in the world, interested in literature, interested in philosophy.

"I can't say I realised that he was going to be quite as successful as he's been because he wasn't a show-off.

"He was very quietly spoken, a pleasant character and really, we're very proud of him at the college."

When the markets opened, shares in Anthropic started at $110 , well above the initial public offering of $83.

articles.title: US Lawmakers Warn Nvidia Scandal Exposes A Bigger AI Threat
articles.summary: Two congressman — one Republican and one Democrat — said they're increasingly concerned over Chinese access to advanced American AI technology.
articles.body:
The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang is rapidly becoming something bigger than the usual corporate leadership scandal. At the Aspen Cyber Summit, two members of the US House Select Committee on China from opposite sides of the aisle raised serious questions about the company's handling of sensitive AI technology, the effectiveness of US export controls and the extent to which advanced computing resources may have reached China.

Both lawmakers also voiced opposition to Huang returning as Nvidia's CEO, while Democratic Rep. Greg Stanton, a Democrat from Arizona, went further, calling for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to be removed over his handling of the matter.

The stakes go beyond Nvidia's leadership crisis. With billions of dollars flowing into AI chips and data centers around the world, lawmakers are questioning whether American technology companies and government regulators can adequately track and control access to the computing resources driving the AI boom. The issue is not just whether restricted processors are shipped to China. Chinese companies may be able to access powerful American AI computing resources remotely through cloud infrastructure in other countries, potentially circumventing restrictions designed to protect US technological advantages.

Can the United States maintain its current AI advantage over China when advanced computing power can be rented across borders, even if the chips themselves never leave an approved location? With congressional investigations around AI and Nvidia intensifying, and new federal restrictions on overseas access to AI computing power taking effect, the Nvidia scandal is putting America's approach to controlling advanced AI technology to the test.

Congress Doesn't Want Jensen Huang Back at Nvidia

At the Aspen Cyber Summit this week in Washington, Republican Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, and his House colleague Stanton took a remarkably bi-partisan position on Nvidia's leadership crisis.

At the panel moderated by The New York Times cybersecurity and intelligence reporter Dustin Volz, both lawmakers expressed opposition to Huang returning as CEO.

"My advice to the board is: don't do it," Stanton said when asked whether Nvidia should consider reinstating Huang.

Moolenaar voiced similar concerns, saying Huang now faces a serious credibility problem that could compromise his effectiveness as the company's leader. He acknowledged Huang's accomplishments building Nvidia into an AI industry powerhouse but questioned whether he could still serve as an appropriate example for the company.

articles.title: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
articles.summary: Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use. It’s rolling out in English for users in the US.
articles.body: Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale. Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US. Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
articles.summary: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information.
articles.body: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time. When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon. Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement. The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door. Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm. Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.
